cells.tense: The person is tending a thing and seeing the whole pattern of it at the same time.
cells.ask: Name what the thing you're tending is turning into, then step back and leave it be for a week to turn into that by itself.
cells.core:
You look after something and you can tell what it's becoming. Not only the daily upkeep — the full shape, where it started, how far it's come, where it's still going. Most people stand too close to their own work for that. You don't.

Care and clear sight work as a pair here. You're patient with the timing, careful with the thing, and you can also stand back and take in the whole of it, which is what makes your care land. You've built some of this already. You can also tell it's time to trust the thing a little more than your hands. What comes next isn't finishing it. It's letting what you've made stand on its own and watching that with the attention you've been giving the making. That part is harder, and it's still yours.
cells.sheetLine: You tend it and you see the whole shape of it.
cells.verb: tending something material and watching how it actually grows

cells.tense: The person will keep pushing the thing toward a version it isn't ready for yet.
cells.ask: Write down the stage the thing is actually in right now, then leave it untouched for one day.
cells.core:
You can already make out what this turns into, and past today there's a finished shape of it, working. So your hands keep moving toward that one — more than the thing can hold yet, more than it needs from you yet. Every check turns into a nudge.

Making out the whole pattern isn't the trouble. Aiming the whole pattern at the small thing you're tending is what's costing you. Care that clutches stops anything from growing, including you. The picture is safe in your hands. The thing in front of you is further back along that path than the picture is, and it needs the kind of attention that will let it sit still a while. It's noticing where the thing is now, not where it will be. That's a different pair of eyes, and you have them.

cells.tense: The person has been tending things while stopping short of the whole pattern.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and write what it's grown into from its start to today, keeping the question open as you go.
cells.core:
You're tending things. You water what's in front of you, you sort what's in front of you, and the longer view doesn't arrive, so each day stands alone. The care is here. What would let it add up isn't, and it's been that way a while.

Looking clearly at what's right in front of you is the same ability as looking clearly at a whole life. Yours stops at the near edge, and you've had your reasons, which are yours and not for anyone else to name. What's missing is a second pair of eyes on your own work — the ones that say this has grown this far. Without it the hands keep moving and nothing settles. That's the part running low. Charge something that belongs to you instead, something that's yours to look at from your own center.

cells.tense: The person is already reading the whole course of a thing and calling it just following the steps.
cells.ask: Say out loud that you saw what this needed and did it, about one recent move, with no explanation after.
cells.core:
You can already tell how a thing develops — where it started, what it needs next, which parts to leave alone. You read that straight off the thing, and you act on it before anyone says what to do. Then you describe it as though the thing were deciding everything and you were keeping up.

What you read is real and it's been running a long time. The name you give it isn't. You've set the pace more than once in a way that doesn't call attention to itself, and keeping it unnamed is what makes the caring tiring — you carry all of it and take credit for none of what you decided. It's saying that the reading was yours, out loud, once. Anyone watching would say the moving was yours anyway.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is the line in the Too Little cell about refusing to see the whole when it looked like a verdict — the record only says the seat starves, not that anything was ever seen and declined, so that clause now runs on pattern-sorting in the present and could be dropped without loss. A reader could object that nothing is starving, they simply have no pattern to see yet, and the ask survives that objection because writing down what was watched is useful whether the capacity is blocked or thin. The sentence that serves me is 'you have been tending things while declining to see what they add up to', which is tidier than the evidence and was cut.
